content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I made a quick assessment of this paper.
content.review:
Summary: This work looks at knowledge distillation: using a large teacher model to train a smaller student model that could have, in this case, as little as 62x fewer parameters. They look at BERT models and propose two ideas to improve effectiveness of knowledge distillation: dual training (encouraging alignment between the teacher and student wordpiece embeddings) and shared variable projection (aids in direct layer wise transfer to the student model).

Positives: Model compression is important, especially for cases like BERT where models are massive. There are lots of works that work on similar things showing that compression is possible for these sorts of models, so studying best practices is an important area of research. The overall experimentation, idea development, and execution shows promise in both techniques.

Concerns: I think the work is a great start of a line of research but don't think the experimentation has enough threads to weave together to tell a super convincing story. I'd like to see an investigation of different ways of compression rather than just at the hidden dimension level. What happens if you vary the number of layers? What happens if you compress non-uniformly for each layer, keeping later layers less compressed.

Overall I think this paper requires more experimentation and analysis to be complete.

content.title: Response to Comments
content.comment:
We are thankful to the reviewer for their comments on how we can make the submission better. We would humbly like to point out to the reviewer that our major contribution, as we see it, is to reduce the WordPiece vocabulary size for the student model, a factor that has generally been overlooked in model distillation prior-art. The hidden state reduction angle, while central to the model compression ratios we report, have been covered to some extent in prior papers - we will be careful to delineate the scope and relative importance of our contributions in a future version. We would also like to argue that our technique can be easily applied on top of existing model distillation techniques for further compression, since existing distillation techniques do not generally change the model vocabulary, and distilling already-distilled models has been successfully done before.

While we do not report this in the paper, we tried reducing the number of layers (from 12 to 6 and 8) for student models trained with dual training only, but obtained significantly worse results without a justifiably significant reduction in the model size. Our variable projection method, in its current shape, may not trivially allow altering the number of layers, but indeed varying the number of layers, in the current framework as well as by exploring other ways of aligning the student and teacher models (e.g. via layerwise pooled outputs) indeed constitute future work on our radar.

Variably compressing different layers in the model - this is indeed a highly interesting approach to further optimizing the model architecture, but at the same time, the difficulty of searching through massively many combinations of compression ratios for different layers, in our opinion, makes such an approach out of scope for this contribution. That said, we are excited by the possibilities here, and have work planned on marrying neural architecture search / reinforcement learning techniques to select model parameters with (variants) of the approach presented here.

content.experience_assessment: I have read many papers in this area.
content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
Summary:
This paper aims to compress the size of large pretrained BERT models for faster inference and cheaper storage. Their method is based on knowledge distillation into a smaller student BERT architecture that has a smaller vocabulary, as well as smaller embedding and hidden dimensions. Their method has 2 steps: 1) dual training which randomly chooses tokens from the sequence to segment using the student vocabulary, and the rest of the tokens are segmented using the teacher vocabulary, as well as 2) shared linear projection layers to align the trainable parameters of student and teacher models by minimizing l2 loss. They present experimental results showing that they can compress BERT base by up to 60x with only a small decrease in accuracy.

Strengths:
- This paper comes at an important time where larger models have been shown to achieve strong performance while requiring too many resources to train and evaluate. This paper makes a step towards smaller models that retain performance while enabling faster inference and cheaper storage.
- The paper is generally well-written and easy to understand. Figure 1 was really helpful.
- The authors evaluate on several downstream tasks and show that compression can be achieved while retaining performance, outperforming the knowledge distillation method proposed in [8].

Weaknesses:
- The novelty is somewhat limited as compared to [8], essentially the difference is to also vary the vocab used between student and teacher models, and also to use up and down projections for knowledge distillation in case the intermediate layer dimensions are different (in which simple matching does not work).
- Why is a random subset of words segmented using the student vocabulary? Since the student model has a much smaller vocab size, it seems to make sense that common words are 'selected' by the student model and segmented, while rare words that are not important in masked language modeling or downstream tasks are not used in the student model, similar to [1,2] where common words are used in the vocab for language modeling and remaining words ignored. Could you expand more on the design decisions here?
- One concern I have is the lack of comparisons with other approaches that do not use knowledge distillation but are still relevant in terms of reducing the vocab size/model parameter size. For example, [1,2] consider only modeling the common words (wordpieces/subwords in this case) for language modeling. A similar approach could be used to train a student BERT model with distillation to a smaller vocabulary. Likewise, you cite many related papers on quantization but do not compare to the performance of quantizing pre-trained BERT models and only storing the quantized weights for downstream tasks. There are also papers that studying reducing the vocab size/embedding matrix using low-rank approximations [3,4], codebook learning [5,6], and dropout [7]. I believe these are all fair comparisons. The only comparison is to [8].
- There are some ablation studies to show that both dual training and shared projection layers are important. However, from Table 3, there are certain datasets and compression factors where only using DualTrain gives best performance.
- From the experimental results, it is inconclusive as to whether shared up or down projection is preferred. Equation (4) simply says L_p, and not whether up or down projection was specifically better, so I'm assuming the authors tried both.  From Table 3 the results are quite inconclusive. It seems unreasonable to train 2 models and take the better one, so I was wondering whether the authors had any intuitions on which one in different settings.

[1] Luong et al. Effective approaches to attention-based neural machine translation, EMNLP 2015
[2] Chen et al. Compressing neural language models by sparse word representations, ACL 2016
[3] Nam and Quoc. Integrating low-rank approximation and word embedding for feature transformation in the high-dimensional text classification, 2017
[4] Grachev et al., Compression of recurrent neural networks for efficient language modeling, 2019
[5] Shu and Nakayama. Compressing word embeddings via deep compositional code learning, ICLR 2018
[6] Chen et al., Learning k-way d-dimensional discrete codes for compact embedding representations, ICML 2018
[7] Chen et al., How large a vocabulary does text classification need? A variational approach to vocabulary selection, NAACL 2019
[8] Sun et al. Patient knowledge distillation for bert model compression, arXiv 2019

content.title: Response to Comments
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their comments and suggestions to improve the paper as well as the references which we will add to a future version. We have responded to the comments individually below.

Comment: The novelty is somewhat limited as compared to [8]...
Response: We believe this work is sufficiently novel among papers discussing BERT model distillation since reducing the vocabulary size for a BERT model has not been looked at in prior related work to the best of our knowledge, and applying standard distillation techniques is nontrivial owing to the nature of the masked language modeling task, which is central to the BERT training procedure. Furthermore, our techniques can be applied in conjunction with nearly all prior BERT distillation methods - this is a point we will elucidate upon more clearly in a future version.

Comment: Why is a random subset of words segmented using the student vocabulary?...
Response: The critical difference between [1, 2] and WordPiece vocabularies is that the WordPiece vocabularies are generated from the training corpora such that all words in the input are representable as sequences of WordPiece tokens i.e. no words are OOV. Thus, instead of being included in the vocabulary directly, rare words representations obtained from more common WordPiece tokens. The set of WordPiece tokens for a given training corpus is generated using a greedy algorithm that minimises the total length of the corpus, in WordPiece token terms. This in practice means that all WordPieces are assigned roughly equal importance, and many common words are natively included in the WordPiece vocabularies for both teacher and student models.

Random words are selected to be chosen to split using the student vocabulary since all embeddings for the student WordPiece tokens need to be learned, and to ensure that all student WordPiece vocabulary tokens are represented in the gradients, we postulate we cannot do much better than randomly selecting input words to be split up using the student vocabulary.

Comment: ...A similar approach could be used to train a student BERT model with distillation to a smaller vocabulary.
Response: (assuming the reviewer meant ‘without distillation’ going by the first sentence in this paragraph) In a way, the suggested approach is akin to using fewer building blocks to represent the entire training data words, which using a smaller WordPiece vocabulary, coupled with the nature of the WordPiece selection algorithm, achieves this automatically. These experiments of ours, with smaller student vocabularies and no knowledge distillation, underperform compared to using knowledge distillation as proposed in our paper.

Comment: ...do not compare to the performance of quantizing pre-trained BERT models…
Response: We refrained from comparing directly with quantization-based approaches since these, in our opinion, belong to an entirely different family of approaches and, perhaps more importantly, very easily be combined with our distillation technique. We will surely keep in mind to include comparable results from quantization approaches, to provide a window into the theoretically-possible higher compression rates from combinations of different approaches.

Comment: There are also papers that studying reducing the vocab size/embedding matrix using low-rank approximations [3,4], codebook learning [5,6], and dropout [7]
Response: These are interesting and relevant papers indeed, and concurrent work (https://openreview.net/forum?id=H1eA7AEtvS) indeed does something like this. Having said that, our work may still not be comparable enough with these approaches since our paper is centered around reducing the vocabulary size of these models, which the aforementioned papers generally do not alter. We will definitely, however, present an analysis in a future version.

Comment: ...certain datasets and compression factors where only using DualTrain gives best performance…
Response: We found that the entire training procedure turns out to be somewhat task dependent in this regard - DualTrain was consistently helpful, but the impact of variable projection was less clear when it came to downstream task performance but not so for the masked language modeling pretraining task. Other ways of aligning the teacher and student models (e.g. aligning layerwise pooled outputs) may alleviate this ambiguity, and are on our radar as future work.

Comment: ...From Table 3 the results are quite inconclusive…
Response: In general, we found that up projection worked generally better than down projection - though the exact order is still task dependent. This may be due to the loss term having lower variance since it is being calculated over a larger space in the former case. Further, we are sanguine that other ways to match the student and teacher models (which are applicable to our changed-vocabulary setting) should help resolve this ambiguity and also provide better downstream task results.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
This paper proposes techniques for improving the compression rate of Knowledge Distillation on BERT models. There are two main ideas. The first is the reduction of the parameter by reducing the vocabulary size of WordPiece model. The observation that a large fraction of parameters in BERT are dedicated to WordPiece embeddings is interesting, as this hasn't received much attention in other works on BERT compression. The second idea is to add a loss function that measures the difference of parameters between teacher and student in the learned projection space. These two ideas are quite complementary in that one can apply one idea to vanilla knowledge distillation without having to apply another simultaneously.

My major concern on this paper is that experiments are not designed to measure the impact of each design choice. First, it is unclear whether DualTrain-based methods outperform PKD with 3 layers because having more layers is more advantageous than having more hidden dimensions. While PKD doesn't straightforwardly allow different hidden dimensions between teacher and student, it is a reasonably straightforward idea to train a shared projection matrix to enable it; concurrent work https://openreview.net/forum?id=rJx0Q6EFPB actually does that. If this was considered as too significant extension of PKD, then authors should've experimented with vanilla knowledge distillation with fewer hidden dimensions. Second, DualTrain-based models have both smaller vocabulary size and smaller hidden dimension size, and it is unclear which one played the greater role in successful distillation.

I would suggest authors to carefully set up baselines that we shall precisely measure the impact of each design choice.  Vanilla knowledge distillation with the same vocabulary as teacher and smaller hidden units shall allow us to understand the impact of decreasing hidden units. By comparing this with DualTrain models with the same vocabulary size, we shall now understand the benefit of decreasing the WordPiece vocabulary size.

Authors make a very insightful note in the discussion that smaller WordPiece vocabulary would imply longer sequence lengths, which may degrade the performance of BERT models. This is an interesting observation, and authors should not avoid running experiments on tasks with longer sequences because it is likely to have negative results. By actually running experiments and breaking down metrics with different sequence length buckets, the research community shall better understand the impact of vocabulary size and the paper will be made stronger.

Minor comments:

1) Table 3 is somewhat difficult to understand because each approach is making a different tradeoff between accuracy and model size. Plotting the accuracy metric vs. model size curve may more effectively visualize the tradeoff.

2) I don't think the variable C in equation 3 was defined. Since there are two vocabularies, it might be useful to clarify the variable and clarify whether there is a loss function for words in teacher vocabulary.

content.title: Response to Comments
content.comment:
We’re thankful to the reviewer for their insightful comments and suggestions to improve the paper. Responses to the comments are below:

Comment: First, it is unclear whether DualTrain-based methods outperform PKD with 3 layers…
Response: We tried to train 8 and 6-layer student models with dual training only, but obtained worse results. While there is merit in claiming that comparing with PKD models with fewer layers is not exactly apples-to-oranges, we believe that the merits of the two approaches could still be compared along the axis of compression ratios. We agree that matching pooled outputs instead of model weights may yield better results while being more flexible, and was/is indeed planned future work in just the manner proposed in the comment.

Comment: Second, DualTrain-based models have both smaller vocabulary size and smaller hidden dimension size, and it is unclear which one played the greater role in successful distillation...
Response: We plan on including results from an experiment with the student model possessing the same hidden dimensions as the teacher but a smaller WordPiece vocabulary to more clearly demonstrate the impact of reducing the vocabulary size alone. The impact of reducing the hidden state sizes alone can be found in prior work and delineated better in a future version, since we believe our core contribution is the former.

Comment: ...authors should not avoid running experiments on tasks with longer sequences because it is likely to have negative results…
Response: While our decision to not experiment with tasks with longer sequences was not driven by the aforementioned concern about longer sequences leading to poorer results, we do acknowledge that the effect does need to be accounted for in experiments, since a smaller WordPiece vocabulary leads to longer sequences and potentially more information truncated, unless the maximum sequence length is corrected to account for this. We can analyze this better in the future version with experiments with the model sequence length, as well as by varying the WordPiece vocabulary size.

Comment: Table 3 is somewhat difficult to understand…
Response: We are thankful for the suggestion, and will include such a plot in a future version.

Comment: I don't think the variable C in equation 3 was defined…
Response: Thanks for bringing this up. C can refer to a student vocabulary token as well as a teacher vocabulary token, since while running the teacher model with mixed-vocabulary inputs, the masked token can belong to either vocabulary. We will be clearer in a future version.
